Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the options for soft-tissue defect coverage on the reconstructive ladder.
Explain the rationale for selecting a specific soft-tissue coverage method for the various types
of fingertip injuries.
Discuss sketch incisions required for cross-finger, reverse cross-finger, and Moberg flaps.
Categorize and describe advancement, rotational, regional, pedicle, and free flaps.
Review specific surgical coverage options for soft-tissue defects of the tibia involving the
proximal, middle, and distal one-third of the leg, including options for coverage over an
exposed total knee arthroplasty implant.

1/31

Considerations regarding the defect to be manage include the following:
Status and type of tissue at the base of the defect (eg, exposed bone, tendon, nerves, or
vessels)
Location of the defect (eg, weight-bearing or highly mobile area)
The duration the defect has been present
Status and type of tissue at the base of the defect
Skin grafts cannot be placed directly on the following:
Bone
Tendon without paratenon
Areas requiring secondary surgery or mobility of soft tissues.
Location of defect and anticipated functional demands (movement, weight bearing)
Colonization or infection
Adequate vascular supply in the wound bed
Availability of healthy local tissue around the defect
Availability of distant tissue if no local tissue is available.
The reconstructive ladder—Select the simplest means with a high likelihood of successful
wound healing (Table 1).
Attempting all the lower rung options is not necessary. Occasionally, a more sophisticated
procedure, such as free tissue transfer, is the best option.
Primary closure—Wound can be closed with acceptable tension.
Healing via secondary intention
Small superficial wounds with no tendon or vessel exposure
In general, results in cosmesis, sensation, and cold tolerance better than flaps with no
donor morbidity
Healing via secondary intention is appropriate, even if a small amount of bone is exposed.
Skin grafts
Split-thickness skin graft (STSG) versus full-thickness skin graft (FTSG)
Occasionally for small sites, grafts may be used directly over bone (eg, distal tuft of the
finger); however, this generally is contraindicated.
Flaps
Definition and considerations
A flap contains its own blood supply.
A flap is used for a defect that:
Cannot or should not be closed primarily (wound bed)
Should not be allowed to heal secondarily (functional demands, contracture)

Cannot support an STSG or FTSG
The donor site can be closed primarily or covered with an STSG.
Flap categories
Region
Local and regional flaps: adjacent tissue
Distant flaps: tissue from another site
Vascularity
Random pattern (no vascular pedicle)
Axial or pedicle flaps (designed around a blood vessel)
Free flap: an axial flap in which the blood vessels are divided and reconnected at a
distant site

3/31

Wounds with bacterial counts higher than 10,000 microorganisms per gram of tissue are
not suitable for skin grafting. Serial débridement to a clean bed free of nonviable tissue
and bacteria also is important for the health of rotational and free flaps. Muscle flaps are
the best choice in the presence of bacterial colonization or infection because they are
associated with a higher survival rate than random pattern flaps or fasciocutaneous
flaps
A key factor of a flap is that it brings vascularity independent of the recipient site defect
for viability. Dissimilar from a skin graft, in which viability is dependent on ingrowth of
vessels from a recipient bed, a flap has a vascular supply independent from the recipient
bed allowing healing to occur (Video 1).
Video 1 Carey JN: Keys to successful flap transfer, from Carey J, mod: How to raise basic
free flaps safely for orthopaedic trauma. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Technique
Healing by Secondary Intention
Appropriate débridement of contaminated or nonviable tissues.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
4/31

Judicious use of antibiotic agents: uncommonly helpful; open wounds are not prone to
infection.
Petroleum jelly over the open wound to keep the tissues moist.
Dressing is applied.
Wound is washed with soap and water daily and re-dressed.
Large defects may take several weeks to heal.
Skin Grafting
Overview
STSG
Movement of part of the epidermis and dermis from a healthy site to cover a wound.
FTSG
Movement of the epidermis and dermis from a healthy site to cover a wound.
FTSG contains hair follicles and sweat glands.
Physiology
Initial survival of the graft depends on imbibition.
The graft passively absorbs oxygen and nutrients from the wound bed.
Within a few days inosculation occurs.
The cut vessels on the underside of the skin graft and the capillary beds in the wound bed
connect, establishing a vascular connection.
The graft becomes adherent over 7 to 10 days.
Indications
A wound that cannot be closed primarily and is too large for secondary intention.
Suitable vascular bed.
Free of infection or excessive bacterial colonization.
Contraindications
Incomplete excision of malignancy such as skin cancer.
Infection.
Bleeding that would compromise healing of the graft.
Seroma and hematoma can limit adherence and vascular supply from the underlying bed.
Exposed bone or absent paratenon
STSG can be considered after 2 to 3 weeks of healing under a bilayer collagen membrane
covered with a layer of silicone.
Dressings that encourage adherence
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
5/31

The graft is applied without laxity or folds.
Multiple sutures are placed at the edges of the graft and tied over a moist cotton bolster on
top of petroleum gauze to limit shear forces.
As an alternative, a vacuum sponge can be used.
The bolster is removed after 1 week or longer.

Technique
A collagen membrane can be placed over vessels, nerves, small areas of bone, and
tendon without paratenon. The patient’s own cells and tissues (fibroblasts, lymphocytes,
macrophages, and capillaries) migrate into the membrane. For areas smaller than 1 cm2,
the silicone can be removed at 2 to 3 weeks and treated with silver sulfadiazine until
epithelization. Larger defects covered with collagen membrane receive a STSG 2 to 3
weeks after placement.
To ensure direct contact between bed and graft, a bolster is particularly important over a
defect that is concave and occasionally can be omitted if grafting a convex surface.
Split-Thickness Skin Grafting
Contraindication: contraction may limit motion; use a FTSG instead.
Selection of donor site
Area without pressure when sitting or lying down
Area of thick dermis (eg, anterolateral thigh)
Timing
Based on potential for colonization
Grafting (within 2 to 3 days) may limit bacterial colonization.
Alternatively, débride the wound of devitalized tissue and wait for early granulation tissue,
which represents an adequately vascular and decolonized bed.
Thickness
Thin (0.005 to 0.012 inches)
Intermediate (0.012 to 0.018 inches)
Thick (0.018 to 0.03 inches)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
6/31

Advantage: less contraction than via secondary intention healing
Disadvantages: hair follicles and sweat glands
Meshing: STSGs can be meshed to increase the area of the defect that can be covered and to
allow for drainage of potential hematoma.

Split-Thickness Skin Grafting
If an STSG is raised, the donor wound heals via re-epithelialization. Epithelial cells
migrate from the remnants of the underlying dermis across the wound bed. If a thicker
graft is harvested from thinner skin, correspondingly less dermis is present for re-
epithelialization and will heal poorly; therefore, areas of relatively thick skin, such as the
anterolateral thigh, should be selected.
Full-Thickness Skin Grafting
Utility
More durable and wear-resistant than STSGs
Less contraction
Transfer all the afferent nerve endings and skin adnexa located in the subcutaneous tissue
May provide better reinnervation and, therefore, better sensation than STSGs
Remove underlying subcutaneous fat

Full-Thickness Skin Grafting
FTSGs provide more durable, flexible coverage than STSGs. Grafts preferentially are
harvested from hairless or nearly hairless areas. Hair will grow at the recipient site in a
manner similar to that in which hair would grow at the donor site. This should be
considered when harvesting skin from the inguinal area in a child in whom hair will grow
at the new recipient site after adolescence. Because direct contact to the underlying bed
is important for vascularization of the graft, a bolster applying gentle pressure over graft
can be used. The graft should be defatted, with care taken to maintain the thickness of
SEND FEEDBACK

7/31

the graft but to remove any subcutaneous tissue that may compromise the ability of the
graft to survive.
Flaps
Local Flaps
Random Pattern Flap
A random pattern local skin flap does not contain an axial vessel.
The length-to-width ratio should be no greater than 2:1 to prevent vascular compromise.
The flaps may be described by their geometric shape:
Mitten (bilobed) flap
Limberg (rhomboid) flap
Semicircular rotation
Bipeninsular
Simple unipeninsular advancement
Mobile skin, such as that on the dorsum of the metacarpals, is required.

Random Pattern Flap
The dimensions of a random pattern flap should be tailored to the anatomic area being
managed. A general rule of thumb is that a length-to-width ratio of 1:1 is definitely safe;
this can be extended to 2:1 over the dorsum of the hand but should be more restrictive
in the foot.
Axial Pattern Flap/Pedicle Flap
Has a named artery (pedicle) and its venae comitantes oriented along the long axis of the flap
Axial pattern flaps have better blood supply than random pattern flaps.
Greater resistance against infection
Enables the length-to-width ratio to be substantially greater than 2:1
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
8/31

An axial pattern flap can be fasciocutaneous, muscular, musculocutaneous, osseous,
osteocutaneous, or composite.
A muscle flap can be covered with a skin graft.

Axial Pattern Flap/Pedicle Flap
Advantages of axial pattern flaps include greater resistance to infection than random
pattern flaps. Axial pattern flaps provide larger length-to-width ratios and increased
mobility of the flap compared with simple rotations or advancement. Care must be taken
to preserve the pedicle, and this may limit the ability to thin the flap. For example, an
anconeus flap or a flexor carpi ulnaris flap can be used for
elbow/olecranon/radiocapitellar coverage. The pedicle is posterior and superior to the
descending branch of the profunda brachii.
Island Pattern Flap
An area of skin detached from all its host attachments except for the artery that is perfusing it
and the venae comitantes that are draining it.
A length-to-width ratio is not applicable.
Can reach a more distant recipient site than an axial flap.
Useful for coverage of the dorsum of the hand proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joints.
Common island pattern flaps
Posterior interosseous artery flap
Reverse pedicle radial forearm flap
Perfused by the radial artery and its cutaneous perforators, between the flexor carpi
radialis and the brachioradialis
Radial forearm fascial flap
Perfused by the radial artery and its cutaneous perforators, between the flexor carpi
radialis and the brachioradialis
Radial forearm fascial perforator flap
Uses perforators from the radial artery to the forearm fascia between the radial styloid and
7 cm proximal to the styloid
Ulnar artery flap
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
9/31

Perfused by the ulnar artery and its cutaneous perforators, deep to (ie, radial to) the ulnar
nerve
Becker flap
Perfused by the dorsal branch of the ulnar artery that emerges on the ulnar aspect of the
flexor carpi ulnaris muscle-tendon unit adjacent to the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar
nerve

Island Pattern Flap
The posterior interosseous artery lies between the extensor digiti quinti and the
extensor carpi ulnaris. The main perforators proximally are approximately one-third
between the lateral epicondyle and the distal radioulnar joint. The proximal extent of the
posterior interosseous artery is deep to the anconeus muscle belly along the proximal
ulna. The flap is based on reverse flow into the posterior interosseous artery and its
distal anastomosis with the anterior interosseous artery close to the distal radioulnar
joint.
Distant Flaps
Tissue from another anatomic site.
Indication: if local tissue is of insufficient amount or quality for a local flap.
Distant Random Pattern Flap
Has all the characteristics of a random pattern flap but comes from another site.
Examples are a chest flap and an abdominal flap.
Distant Axial Pattern Flap
Examples
Groin flap: supplied by the superficial circumflex iliac artery.
Latissimus dorsi flap: supplied by the thoracodorsal artery, a branch of the subscapular
artery.
Hypogastric artery flap (Shaw flap): based on the superficial inferior epigastric artery.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
10/31


Distant Flaps
The origin of the superficial circumflex iliac artery is 2 cm below the inguinal ligament on
the lateral aspect of the common femoral artery. The superficial circumflex iliac artery
runs parallel to the inguinal ligament and emerges into superficial subcutaneous tissue
lateral to the sartorius.
The latissimus dorsi muscle also is supplied by perforators from the thoracic intercostal
and lumbar arteries that allow for its use as a pedicle flap.
The superficial inferior epigastric artery arises from a common trunk with the superficial
circumflex iliac artery from the femoral artery or from the femoral artery directly. The
flap may be raised in a transverse or proximal-distal orientation.
Free Tissue Transfer
An axial or island pattern flap that is supplied by a recognizable artery and is drained by
recognizable veins is surgically removed from one site (the donor site) and transferred and
revascularized in another site (the recipient site) within the same individual.
The flap is transferred heterotopically using a procedure in which the blood supply is first
divided and then reestablished via microsurgical anastomosis of its arterial supply and
draining veins.
A length-to-width ratio is not applicable.
Indication: if local or distant tissue is of insufficient amount or quality for random, axial, or
island flap transfer.
Can be cutaneous, fasciocutaneous, musculocutaneous, muscular, osseous, or composite.
Functional free tissue transfer
Reconnected to nerves to restore function.
Patients with considerable loss of musculature in the upper extremity.
Perforator Flaps
A fasciocutaneous flap for which the main vascular supply is a musculocutaneous or a
septocutaneous perforator from a named axial vessel.

9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
11/31

Length-to-width ratio may be greater than 2:1 because of the presence of perforator vessels
contained within the flap itself.
Examples include propeller flaps (vary by anatomic area length-to-width ratios of 3:1 but
considered safe), deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps, and posterior tibial artery perforator
flaps.

Coverage Options
Island flaps from the forearm
Axial pattern distant flaps

anterolateral thigh flap
Thumb–index finger web
space reconstruction

FTSG = full-thickness skin graft, STSG = split-thickness skin graft.
Reproduced from Boyer MI: Soft-tissue coverage, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp
1183-1191.
Fingertip
Healing via secondary intention is almost always the best option.
Even if a small amount of bone or tendon is exposed
Typically, the protocol involves keeping the wound clean and the open portion moist, such as
with petroleum jelly.
Early motion of the digit is encouraged.
FTSG is associated with the disadvantage of less sensibility.
Flaps
Volar V-Y advancement flap: useful for transverse or dorsal oblique tip amputations (Figure
1)
Dual lateral digital V-Y advancement flaps
Iselin (flag) flap: useful for stump coverage

9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
13/31

Dorsal skin of the proximal phalanx supplied by the anastomosis between the dorsal
metacarpal artery and the proper digital artery
The most common donor fingers are the index and long fingers.
The Iselin flap is useful for coverage of the volar or dorsal aspect of an adjacent digit or the
volar aspect of the same digit.
Thenar flap: useful for tip coverage of index and long fingers in young patients
Thenar H flap: modification of the thenar flap; same indications as those for the thenar flap.
Free tissue transfer options such as venous flaps or partial toe pulp flaps
Figure 1 Illustrations of a finger show the Atasoy-Kleinert V-Y flap technique. A, The distal edge of
the wound is the base of the flap and the apex of the flap should extend to the distal
interphalangeal crease. The skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fibrous septa are incised (B), and the
flap is secured over the defect with the use of sutures (C). (Reproduced from Lee DH, Mignemi
ME, Crosby SN: Fingertip injuries: An update on management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2013;21[12]:756-766.)

Fingertip
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
14/31

The Atasoy-Kleinert flap is a triangular advancement flap. It is constructed by making a
distally based chevron incision that is then advanced distally and closed in a V to Y
manner. The incision should extend proximally to the distal interphalangeal joint crease
and laterally as far as 2 mm lateral to the nailfold. Depending on the wound requiring
coverage, the Atasoy-Kleinert flap can be advanced as much as 1 cm. Care should be
taken to avoid excessive tension because it may lead to a hooked nail deformity,
increased hypersensitivity, and flap loss. The flap must be freed of fibrous septa along its
radial and ulnar borders to facilitate mobilization. Removal of the nail plate may aid in
distal attachment. Distal attachment may be augmented by securing the distal aspect of
the flap with the use of a Kirschner wire or a hypodermic needle drilled into the distal
phalanx.
Although similar to the Atasoy-Kleinert flap, the Kutler V-Y advancement is performed on
both sides of the digit. Therefore, this flap provides bilateral mid-lateral fingertip tissue,
especially for revision procedures (Figure 2). Kutler flaps can be used for transverse
amputations. Limitations of this flap include the degree of mobilization possible. Each
Kutler flap can be advanced 3 to 4 mm. Therefore, the largest diameter defect at the
fingertip that can be covered is 8 mm. In addition, fingertip sensitivity may be poorer
compared with Atasoy-Kleinert flaps or healing by secondary intention
Figure 2 Illustrations of a finger show the Kutler lateral V-Y flap technique. A,
Advancement flaps are marked on the mid-lateral aspects of the digit. B, The skin,
subcutaneous tissue, and underlying septa are incised, and the flaps are elevated. The
flaps are mobilized longitudinally over the fingertip (C) and secured with the use of loose
sutures (D). (Reproduced from Lee DH, Mignemi ME, Crosby SN: Fingertip injuries: An
update on management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[12]:756-766.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
15/31

The Iselin (or flag) flap is based on vascularity arising from the web space of the donor
finger. Similar to the cross-finger flap, elevation of this flap occurs off the dorsal aspect
of the donor digit just superficial to the extensor paratenon. The flap is raised from the
proximal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal joint to the distal aspect of the web
space from radial to ulnar mid-lateral lines. The vascularity arises from the web space;
therefore, a bridge of soft tissue containing the pedicle must be preserved to allow for
rotation of the flap pivoting on this point. The flap is raised from the dorsum of the
proximal phalanx and can cover an equal area of a neighboring digit or provide coverage
over the volar aspect of the metacarpal head of the donor finger or a neighboring digit.
The donor site is covered with skin graft.
The thenar flap is raised from the thenar eminence, starting just ulnar to the digital
crease. The ring and little fingers require too much flexion to use this flap. The flap is
sutured to the defect and divided 2 weeks after the index procedure.
One limb of the thenar H flap may be used to close the thenar donor site at the time of
flap division.
Flaps for Other Regions of the Finger
Side finger flap
This flap has a blood supply from the ipsilateral digital artery.
It is useful for coverage of volar metacarpophalangeal defects after contracture release.
Iselin (axial flag) flap
Arterialized side finger flap
Useful for coverage of defects over the dorsal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal joint.
The blood supply is provided by the digital artery (the digital nerve is left in situ).
Cross-finger flap
Random pattern flap consisting of the dorsal skin and subcutaneous tissue of a digit
Elevation of the dorsal skin and subcutaneous tissue from the paratenon of the donor finger
Used to cover the volar aspect of the adjacent digit
Can be laterally or distally based (Figure 3)
Can be made sensate using the dorsal branch of the proper digital nerve
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
16/31

Separated from the donor site 2 to 3 weeks after placement
Revascularized from the healing wound edges
The defect is full-thickness skin grafted over the intact extensor tendon epitenon.
Figure 3 Photographs of a finger with an amputation managed via a cross-finger flap. A,
Preoperative photograph shows a partial amputation of the fingertip. B, Intraoperative
photograph of the finger adjacent to the injured finger shows the planned donor site marked. C,
Postoperative photograph shows the cross-finger flap before it is detached from the donor site.
(Reproduced from Lee DH, Mignemi ME, Crosby SN: Fingertip injuries: An update on
management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[12]:756-766.)
Reverse cross-finger flap
Uses dorsal adipofascial tissue, over which an STSG or FTSG can be placed, to cover the
dorsum of an adjacent digit
Elevation of the dorsal dermis and epidermis only, leaving the adipofascial tissue to cover the
extensor tendon
This flap is then covered with a thick STSG, and the donor site is closed primarily.
Homodigital reverse adipofascial turndown flap
This flap can be useful for dorsal oblique amputations.
The axial pattern flap can be used when the base is more than 5 mm proximal to the
proximal extent of the germinal matrix.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
17/31

STSG or FTSG is required for coverage; FTSG may be used if a suitable soft-tissue bed
(extensor epitenon, digital sheath) is present.
Homodigital island or reverse homodigital island flap
Free flap

Flaps for Other Regions of the Finger
The cross-finger flap is a reliable, easily performed flap that can be used to cover the
volar aspect of a neighboring digit. The flap can be raised and inset under local
anesthesia. Cover the donor site with an FTSG that can be harvested from the same
limb. Suturing the skin graft in place before suturing the flap in place makes closure of
the defect adjacent to the recipient digit easier. The flap can be separated 2 weeks after
it is inset. The likelihood of flap viability can be assessed before separation by placing a
digital tourniquet on the donor finger.
The reverse cross-finger flap can be used to cover dorsal defects on a digit adjacent to
the donor finger. The flap can be raised from the dorsum of a middle phalanx and can
extend from the center of the distal interphalangeal joint to the center of the proximal
interphalangeal joint and as far laterally as the midsagittal lines of the donor finger.
The homodigital island flap derives its blood supply from ladder branch arterial flow
from the digital artery on the opposite side of the finger from which the flap was
harvested.
Thumb Tip
Moberg flap (Figure 4)
The Moberg flap is an axial pattern advancement flap comprising volar thumb skin
containing digital arteries and digital nerves.
This flap is possible only because of the robust dorsal vascular supply of the thumb.
Flexion of the interphalangeal joint typically is required for flap advancement. Therefore, loss
of interphalangeal joint hyperextension is common after a Moberg flap procedure.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
18/31

Figure 4 Illustrations of a thumb show the use of a Moberg (thenar advancement) flap. A, A soft-
tissue defect of the thumb is shown. B, A midaxial incision is made on the radial and ulnar sides
of the thumb, extending proximally to the metacarpophalangeal crease. The volar skin flap and
the neurovascular bundles are dissected off the flexor tendon and advanced over the defect. C,
The flap is secured with the use of sutures. (Reproduced from Lee DH, Mignemi ME, Crosby SN:
Fingertip injuries: An update on management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[12]:756-766.)
Volar cross-finger flap
The volar cross-finger flap is obtained from the index finger.
Stiffness of the index finger metacarpophalangeal joint is a complication of the volar cross-
finger flap procedure.
Digital neurovascular flap from the radial aspect of the ring finger
This flap was popularized by Littler.
Donor site complications
Poor circulation to the donor and ulnar adjacent digits
Cold intolerance
Poor two-point discrimination
Lack of cortical reorientation (uncommon)—Touch on the thumb is perceived as touch on
the ring finger.
FTSG
Free flap
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:37 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Coverage
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000513
19/31


Thumb Tip
The Moberg flap cannot be used for lesser digits. In the thumb, the reach of the flap to
the tip can be extended by incising the skin and soft tissues while preserving the
neurovascular bundles at the digital crease. The defect created at the digital crease is
then covered with a skin graft.
Dorsal Aspect of the Thumb
Kite flap
Blood is supplied by the first dorsal metacarpal artery.
The artery lies subfascially on the first dorsal interosseous muscle on its radial aspect.
The flap is raised distal to proximal, and the pedicle contains the fascia of the first dorsal
interosseous muscle, the first dorsal metacarpal artery, two large dorsal veins, and
potentially branches of the radial sensory nerve.
The flap usually reaches only to the thumb interphalangeal joint but can extend distally.
The donor site is grafted with FTSG.
FTSG is useful if suitable extensor epitenon coverage of the first and third dorsal compartment
tendons is present.

Dorsal Aspect of the Thumb
The integrity of the pedicle of the kite flap should be confirmed via Doppler before
elevation of the flap coming from the radial artery distal to the anatomic snuffbox. The
pedicle should not be specifically isolated but raised with surrounding soft tissue to not
damage the venous drainage of the flap.
Forearm and Dorsal Aspect of the Hand
Avoid muscle flaps.
Do not provide a gliding surface for extensor tendons function.

Forearm and Dorsal Aspect of the Hand
The lateral arm flap is supplied by the posterior radial collateral artery. The profunda
brachii divides into the middle collateral and the radial collateral arteries after piercing
the lateral intermuscular septum. The posterior radial collateral artery runs in the
intermuscular septum between the brachioradialis and the triceps. At most, the flap can
be extended 6 cm distal to the elbow.
The radial forearm flap is supplied by the radial artery, which runs between the
brachioradialis and the flexor carpi radialis. The flap may include the forearm fascia, the
brachioradialis, the palmaris longus, and a portion of the radius that is less than 30% of
the diameter of the diaphysis.
The anterolateral thigh flap is supplied by muscular perforators derived from the
descending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery. This branch of the lateral
femoral circumflex artery travels between the rectus femoris and the vastus lateralis on
the surface of vastus intermedius, deep in the septal plane.


Thumb–Index Finger Web Space Reconstruction
If greater length is necessary, four-flap Z-plasty can increase length by 2.6 times. All
limbs of a Z-plasty should be of equal length. Adequate length of flap for transposition
can be assessed by elevating just one limb of the Z-plasty and ensuring that the midpoint
of the elevated chevron can reach the longitudinal line of the Z-plasty. The angles of the
Z-plasty should be measured with the use of a goniometer or an angle template because
visual estimation of the flaps often leads to Z-plasty with more acute angles, which leads
to less lengthening.

Traditionally, free flaps for coverage have had increased survival if performed within the

6 cm of bone should be left cephalad to the mortise to minimize the risk of ankle

The fibular flap can be harvested with the flexor hallucis longus and a skin paddle (skin
supply from peroneal artery perforators emerging from posterior to the fibula). It also
can be harvested with the soleus muscle proximally.
Iliac crest flap
The iliac crest flap is a free tissue transfer based on the deep circumflex iliac artery.
Harvest of the accompanying muscle is possible, but no reliable skin paddle is present.
Superior medial geniculate artery flap
This flap is based on periosteal branches of the superior medial geniculate artery.
A fragment of the distal medial femoral metaphysis (cortical and cancellous bone) is
harvested.
Articular cartilage from the trochlea can be included in the flap.

Bone Flaps
Division of soleus perforators is necessary during harvest. These typically pierce the
soleus muscle adjacent to the lateral intermuscular septum. The peroneal artery arises
from the tibioperoneal trunk, which originates from the popliteal artery after takeoff of
the anterior tibial artery.
The peroneal pedicle for the vascularized fibular graft has a length of 6 to 8 cm and an
arterial diameter of 1.5 to 3 mm. The fibular graft can be cut at its midpoint and through
elevation of the peroneal vascularity to provide a double barrel vascularized graft.
The iliac crest flap is used less commonly than other bone flaps because of the curved
nature of the iliac crest and the thin cortical shell, making it weak in bony reconstruction
using screws and plates. Advantages include a cosmetic scar, the ability to harvest large
amounts of cancellous bone, and the ability for use as a pedicle flap to manage
osteonecrosis of the femoral head;, however, an iatrogenic hernia is possible, so
meticulous closure is important.

The medial femoral condyle flap is based on the descending genicular or medial superior

Tissue Expansion
Tissue expansion results in decreased dermal thickness.
The epidermal thickness increases initially but then returns to baseline.
Collagen bundles in the expanded tissue are longitudinally oriented, orderly, and parallel.

Tissue Expansion
Soft-tissue expansion can be performed to increase the available soft tissue for a
rotational or advancement flap. The process requires a two-stage surgical procedure,
insertion of the soft-tissue expander, and subsequent removal and advancement of the
expanded tissue. The soft-tissue expander is a silicon balloon connected to an injection
port that is tunneled subcutaneously to be away from the expander. The expanded
tissue can be used to replace scarred or contracted adjacent tissue. To allow for
incisional healing and prevent implant exposure or extrusion, inflation of the soft-tissue
expander is delayed until 3 weeks after implant placement. Weekly inflations with saline
are subsequently carried out until the desired expansion is reached. Expansion is limited
by overlying tissue vascularity, patient pain, and undue tension on peri-implant incisions.
Approximately 2 to 3 weeks after final expansion, which allows for tissue stretch
relaxation, the second stage of implant removal and tissue advancement is performed.
Complications may include infection, neuropraxia of nearby nerves, implant exposure or
extrusion, overlying skin ischemia, and implant leakage. Complications are more
common in the lower extremities.

VAC devices use a nonadherent sponge and intermittent or continuous suction in a closed
system.
The negative pressure of the VAC results in the following:
Decreased edema
Stimulated vascular ingrowth
Decreased bacterial contamination
Activated tissue growth via cell deformation
Leads to protein and matrix molecule production
VAC devices can be used for the following:
Definitive wound closure
In preparation for flap coverage (encourage granulation, decreased colonization)
Postoperatively over flaps or grafts

Vacuum-Assisted Closure Device
VAC devices can be easily used without the need for surgical skills of flap or graft
coverage. The granulation tissue produced is less pliable than most flap coverage and,
therefore, is better for diaphyseal areas. Before flap coverage, a VAC device may be used
to decrease bacterial contamination for a period of 1 week. After flap coverage, a VAC
device may be applied over the flap to decrease postoperative edema.
